content.thinking:
I'm planning a Genshin-style red panda on a mossy stone using the toon kit components -- cel shading, fur edges, anime eyes, ink lines, and glow effects -- and considering whether the anime eye style suits a red panda's features while writing the module carefully since I can't test it directly.

Rather than use the standard animeEye component, I'll draw a custom eye with big round dark iris, colored highlights, and the panda's characteristic tear-mark shading since the lash flicks on the preset eye read as too humanoid. For the pose, I'm leaning toward a bipedal balancing stance -- standing upright on hind legs with arms outstretched like a tightrope walker, tail raised in an S-curve for counterbalance -- which reads clearly as "balancing" on the rounded mossy stone.

I'm roughing out proportions: a stylized ~0.75m standing height on a ~0.25-0.3m flat-topped boulder (width 0.7, built with a faceted lathe profile and moss tufts/ferns on top), with the panda's feet planted at the stone's top surface around y=0.30, and now I'm working out the leg and ankle coordinates to connect the body chain upward from there.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy -- hips, spine chain rising from the hips up through chest, neck, and chibi-proportioned head -- placing approximate joint coordinates so the total height (panda plus stone) lands around 0.9-1.15m with a slightly forward lean.

I'll tilt the body slightly forward for a natural red panda posture, defining the hip joint and spine chain with catmull-rom coordinates, then building out the torso loft with bone stations along that spine path.

I'm worried the round cap bottom extends too far below the hips, leaving legs looking too short relative to the feet position. Let me reshape the body radius as a pear profile—wider at the belly/hip and narrower at the chest—so the torso bottom lands around y=0.36 to 0.37, giving the thighs enough visible length starting from the hip sockets.

Setting head radius and total height around 1.16m, checking that body-to-head proportions stay chibi-like. Now working out the leg joint chain with hip, knee, and ankle positions for an IK-based limb setup on each side.

I'm working out the foot geometry so the toe tip sits at the right height relative to the stone surface, letting the paw sink just slightly for contact rather than floating or clipping through. Then I'm calculating the leg segment lengths needed to span from the hip down to the ankle given the vertical drop.

For the plantigrade stance, I'm making sure the sole lies flat since red pandas walk with full foot contact, and adding a small cluster of toe spheres with darker paw coloring at the front of each foot.

For the arms, I'm positioning them outstretched for balance with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw-tip joints on each side, using coordinates that angle slightly up and back, with tapering radii and dark brown coloring consistent with a red panda's limb coloring.

I'm working out the paw details with small toe nubs and tiny cream claws, then moving to the head and neck setup, placing the head joint above the spine with a short neck joint chain connecting them.

Now I'm building the head shape itself, positioning its center and scaling a wide sphere for the skull plus a shorter protruding ellipsoid for the cream muzzle.

I'm planning the smaller facial details: a dark triangular nose, flaring cream cheek tufts shaped as pointed spikes, rust-colored ears with cream inner fur, and white brow spots. For the eyes and the characteristic tear-mark stripes, I'm thinking of painting them directly onto the head as decals or texture positioned relative to the head's center rather than building them as separate geometry.

Writing paint shader logic...

Defining the full color palette...

Now I'm thinking about the body coloring itself — real red pandas have dark chests/bellies against rust backs, so I want to use a fur-edge gradient with a dark chocolate underside transitioning to rust, zigzagging along the body axis to mimic fur texture at the boundary.

For the tail, I'm plotting a curving S-shaped path from hips upward and back, checking it clears the stone's height, and tapering its radius from thick at the base to thin at the tip for a bushy ringed look, with six chained segments named tail1 through tail6 parented to the hips.

I'm also scattering fur-tuft cards along the tail for silhouette texture, colored rust, and considering a small Genshin-style magical accessory for the panda—maybe a tiny glowing leaf sprout or charm resting on its head to keep that cute, cel-shaded ornamental feel without cluttering the scene.

Instead of that, I'll lean into the stone itself: adding mossy tufts with small glowing blue-green mushrooms or flowers along its edge, Dendro-inspired but modest in number, skipping the leaf-on-head idea for simplicity. Now I'm defining the panda's head geometry and proportions in code.

For the eyes, I'm positioning them as decals on the head sphere at a symmetric azimuth and elevation, sizing them around 0.07 by 0.08, and designing a custom eye texture with a prominent highlight that I'll keep consistent on the same side for both eyes to read naturally to the viewer.

Placing more head details...

I'll simplify and just place the nose directly with coordinates, sinking it slightly into the muzzle, and add a tiny white highlight sphere for a cute shine effect. For the mouth, I'm splitting it into an upper jaw (the muzzle) and a separate cream-colored lower jaw ellipsoid positioned beneath it, possibly adding a curved smile line between them.

For the muzzle lines, I'm thinking of draping thin ink-colored curves along the surface -- a philtrum line descending from the nose and branching outward into a "w" shape for the mouth corners, built as catmull-rom paths swept with thin rod geometry and lifted slightly off the skin surface so they read as ink marks rather than geometry.

I'll keep the smile line modest and skip adding a tongue, but plan small dark dot spheres scattered on the muzzle for whiskers, maybe three per side, placed via the same surface draping approach.

For ears, I'm designing red panda-style ears: large, rounded-triangular, tilted outward, rust-colored outside with cream fringe inside, extruded as a mirrored outline in the facing plane with thickness along the depth axis.

Working out ear orientation vectors...

For s=-1, computing x×y actually flips the normal to point backward instead of forward, so the mirrored ear would face the wrong way. I need a different axis convention that keeps the thickness direction consistent across both mirrored copies, rather than naively flipping x.

Simpler approach: shift the inner cream extrude's center forward slightly so it peeks out past the ear's front face while staying tucked inside the back, with a smaller scaled-up offset outline for the inner patch. I'll make the ear outer color rust with a cream inner and consider pale tufts for realism, then parent these ear parts rigidly to the head bone.

For facial details, I'm placing small cream eyebrow dots as flattened stick-ons at set azimuth and elevation points on the head surface, and adding cream cheek-ruff tufts as outward-angled spikes near the lower sides of the head using similar hit-point placement logic.

Thinking about overall accessory richness now—considering whether a small decorative touch like a leaf scarf would fit the Genshin dendro aesthetic, though it's not strictly necessary.

I'm adding a Liyue-style neck collar instead: a red cord with a gold bell and tassel, positioned as a horizontal ring around the neck area where the body meets the head, working out the loop geometry so it sits correctly at the base of the neck without being hidden by the head.

For the stone, I'll shape it as a lathed form with a faceted outline — a slightly irregular profile tapering from a wide base up to a flattened dome around 0.27 in height, with low segment count for a rough, mossy-rock feel.

I'll make the top a flat disc at y=0.27 so all nine triangles sit level, with feet resting at 0.268. For asymmetry, rather than risk scaling the lathe mesh non-uniformly after paint is baked, I'll add extra small boulder lumps beside the main stone instead.

I'll place a second smaller lathe (radius 0.18, height 0.18) offset behind-right, plus a tiny pebble, keeping the main stone centered at origin with the panda's feet resting near its narrow top for that balancing look.

Checking the geometry: feet span roughly ±0.14 in x and up to 0.13 in z, giving a radius around 0.19, which fits within the stone's 0.22 top radius while still looking precarious. I'm refining the stone's profile points to get a slightly beveled flat top rather than a perfectly round one, adjusting the coordinates so the rim tapers naturally into the flat surface.

For the surface shading, I'm designing a custom paint function that blends bluish-grey stone ("#7f8aa3") with patches of bright-to-dark moss ("#6fbf3f" to "#3f8f3a") using cel-shaded violet shadows. The moss should favor upward-facing surfaces with some noise-based variation so it reads as natural growth rather than a uniform coat.

I'm also adding scattered moss tuft cards along the top rim and sides for extra texture, using a simple SVG blade-clump graphic repeated around 70 times at a small scale, filtered to appear mostly on upper, slightly elevated surfaces.

Still working out the hanging moss card placement...

I need to keep the moss lumps and surface cards away from the feet region, so I'm filtering placements to only scatter on the sloped rim area (radius beyond ~0.235 from center, with upward-facing normals) and excluding the small zone under the paws.

I'm also checking foot placement geometry: positioning ankle and toe z-coordinates so the farthest foot corner stays within the top disc radius of 0.22, giving enough clearance for the scattered cards and moss to sit without intersecting the panda's legs.

Now I'm working out the IK chain for the legs, setting hip, ankle, and sole targets with thigh/shin/foot segment lengths so the reach distance stays feasible for each limb.

I'm naming the leg chain joints: hip, knee, and ankle for the three spans, with foot as the tip joint at the toe contact point.

For the sweep, I'm using a radius profile that tapers from 0.065 near the hip down to 0.04 at the foot, giving a tapered leg shape with a rounded paw-like end. I need to check that the foot's bottom edge at y=0.26 sits close enough to the ground plane at y=0.27 for proper contact.

For the toes, I'm adding three small spheres offset slightly in x at the foot's tip position to suggest individual toes, with small dark claw accents on top.

For leg color I'm using a dark brownish-black cel tone with a gradient on the thighs shifting from rust to dark, then working out shoulder and arm placement to start the chain path for the arms.

Still defining arm joints...

Still plotting tail curve points...

With 6 points giving 5 spans, I'll paint alternating ring colors along the tail chain—lighter orange and dark russet bands with a darker tip, plus thin ink outlines at each ring boundary for definition.

Now I'm scattering tufted fur elements along the tail's sweep to break up the silhouette, using tapered flame shapes with darkened bases, sized small and oriented to flow toward the tail tip direction.

Instead I'll build a separate tail-position paint that projects each point onto the tail path via closestT and feeds that into a shared ring-color function, so both the sweep and the cards can reuse the same tone logic consistently.

Checking that grey-textured cards tint properly when given a color string or Paint, and that white/grey fill values stay neutral until tinted. I'm also planning to scatter small cream tufts on the head's cheek region using a filtered selection based on position and normal direction, leaning them outward-back, plus modest rust-toned tufts along the body edge to round out the fur detail.

Now I'm thinking through the anime-style stylization: adding eye decals with large highlights, and pink cheek blush ellipses beneath each eye using a radial gradient cut at 0.5 alpha for a hard flat edge, with small hatch lines for an anime blush effect. I'm positioning these decals relative to the head sphere's surface coordinates, placing the eyes at roughly ±30 azimuth and 5 elevation against the head's radii.

Now I'm working out the eye geometry and spacing—sizing each eye around 0.07 by 0.085, separating them with roughly a 27° angle so they sit wide and cute with a small gap, and then figuring the tear mark details flowing down from below each eye using local coordinate offsets on the face.

For the head coloring, I'm sketching out the real raccoon pattern: rusty-brown crown and forehead, cream-white cheeks and muzzle, dark tear streaks, and a pale eyebrow patch. I'm defining the cheek region using a threshold on the local coordinates with a jagged zigzag edge so the fur boundary doesn't look like a clean line.

The back of the head stays rust-colored throughout, while the lower chin region blends into the cream zone. Each region maps to a cel-shaded color function that uses the real surface normal for lighting. For the body, I'm keeping the back rust and the front a dark brown belly, and considering whether a cream chest bib would read better for the red panda's cute stylization.

Settling on a deep brown for the belly instead of a lighter rust-brown, and skipping the cream bib for now. I'm defining the body's cross-section radii along the spine so it bulges slightly at the chest and tapers toward the head and tail, building the shape as a sweep along the spine chain.

Checking proportions: the legs are quite stubby relative to the body and head, but that fits the chibi style, so I'll leave the overall sizing as is rather than stretching the upper body. I'm also considering a subtle hip/belly bulge for a "pants" look, and noting that the chest cap overlaps slightly into the head region, which should be fine given where the head center sits.

Now I'm checking the neck and jaw placement -- the head bottom nearly conceals the neck and collar, and I'm verifying the jaw and muzzle ellipsoids don't clip through the collar or chin area, adjusting their centers and radii slightly to keep everything seated naturally on the shoulders.

Now I'm placing the jaw joint with its forward aim, then working out ear positioning relative to the head's ellipsoid surface—checking that the ear base sits just inside the head sphere at the given offsets and verifying the resulting ear height and tilt direction work geometrically.

I'm also deciding on accessories: skipping sticks or a leaf, instead going with a golden bell collar plus tassel cards and a cord for a Liyue-style knot. For extra detail I'm adding small glowing dendro-blossom flowers scattered across the stone rim and sides using card textures with a glow effect, while skipping glowing eyes or bell glints to keep things simple.

For the mouth, rather than sculpting a 3D shape I'm opting for a decal approach: a small texture applied to the muzzle showing the philtrum line and a simple smile, keeping the jaw closed and letting the nose remain a 3D sphere separate from the mouth decal.

For the decal placement I'm casting rays against the muzzle surface to find attachment points for features like whisker dots and the nose, using ray-hit coordinates near the front-top of the muzzle to position a small dark nose sphere with a highlight, stuck and embedded slightly into the surface.

Now I'm shifting to the skeleton structure, planning out the joint hierarchy: hips as root, spine segments, neck, head, jaw, ear joints attached to the head, plus limb chains for arms, legs, and tail, keeping the total joint count under the 160 limit.

Finishing the neck-to-head coordinates, then I decide head parts should just use absolute model-space positions tied to the head bone rather than local offsets, simplifying orientation since there's no aim needed. I jot down the rest pose has no head rotation, and start listing the texture set: eye, blush, mouth, grey fur tuft, green moss tuft, and flower.

Continuing the texture list, I add a glowing variant, a red/gold tassel, maybe a fern frond card for the stone side, and a small coin-like emblem — avoiding actual text rendering risk by drawing a simple geometric Dendro leaf design on the coin face instead of Chinese characters. That rounds out to about 8-9 textures total, which feels sufficient, and I note the paint groups needed: stone, head, body, tail, leg, arm, muzzle, and ear.

I'm setting up helper functions for building sphere-based parts — a `ball` helper that creates a low-poly sphere geometry attached to a bone with position and scale, so I can reuse it for small round elements like the nose, claws, or bell decoration. I'm thinking about whether smooth sphere geometry will look right under toon shading, since the hard-edged cel shadows depend on normals and a smooth low-poly sphere might not give the faceted look I want.

Now I'm working out how to add fur-like cheek ruffs — planning three flame-shaped or spike-like tufts per side of the face, placed around the cheek at different angles pointing outward and back, considering whether to use extruded tapered blade shapes or simpler cone spikes for this detail.

I'll position the spike bases on the head sphere surface using azimuth/elevation hits for cheek spikes, with bones inherited from head, angling the directions outward and downward. For a cute touch, I'll add a few small rust-colored tufts on the crown of the head, like an ahoge-style forehead tuft.

I'm sweeping a curved bezier path to form one curly tuft on top with rust-colored paint and pointed caps. For colors, I'm using dark brown for legs and hands with a gradient from rust at the shoulders fading to dark along the arms, mirroring the gradient points for left and right sides.

Writing arm paint logic...

Still writing SVG code...

Still defining SVG textures...

For the tassel I'm planning red cords with a gold knot on top and lighter strand highlights. Then I'm sketching the coin emblem as a gold ring with a green leaf motif at its center, and figuring out the bell as a gold sphere with a thin dark slot, hanging with a coin and tassel below it via a small cylinder geometry.

Now I'm defining the collar cord as a red swept tube, and working out how to loop it around just the body cross-section at shoulder height without catching the arms geometry.

I'm then figuring out the coin's placement by raycasting forward from the collar to find the front surface point, offsetting down and out slightly so it hangs naturally below the cord, and planning a small tassel card attached near the coin's base, possibly rigged to a spine bone.

Checking proportions next: collar sits at chest height where the body radius is around 0.105, the head leans slightly forward relative to the body center, and the shoulder joint position falls safely within the body's width at that height so the arm will read as visible rather than clipped.

For the surrounding scene I'm placing a second and third stone using lathe profiles with varying radii and heights, scattered near the base for composition, keeping them away from the tail's higher back position so nothing overlaps awkwardly.

Checking distances, the second stone cluster does overlap the main one, but that's acceptable since it reads as a natural merged rock formation. Now I'm defining the moss and stone coloring, using mottled textures with noise-based shading to give each stone a weathered, lichen-covered look.

Continuing the texture logic, I'm determining crack patterns from cell distances and ensuring flat tops get fully mossed over. I'll add small moss lumps along the rim using tiny icosahedron sticks with their own noise-based coloring, skipping flower details for simplicity.

Now I'm working out how to scatter grass tuft cards across the stone surfaces using upward-facing hit normals, filtering by slope and distance from origin so tufts avoid flat centers and cluster naturally near edges, with cross-faced cards for visibility from all angles.

For the glowing flowers I'm scattering fewer cards (count 7) on surfaces with steeper upward normals, keeping them smaller and upright with cross-faced geometry so the symmetrical petal texture reads properly from front and back rather than disappearing edge-on.

Now I'm checking the rest of the character build: decal placement uses hit-based orientation for eyes with default up alignment and no mirroring, and I'm adding small cream-colored sphere details for eyebrow dots using the stick helper with flat paint colors rather than textures.

For the eyebrow dots, I'm scaling the sphere geometry into an ellipsoid shape before applying it so it sits flattened against the surface, with hit angles computed for azimuth and elevation to make sure they stay visible on the head rather than hidden. I'm skipping extra details like lashes or pants, finalizing the metadata object, and writing the complete code while being careful about unused imports since the type checker will flag them.

Writing import statements...

Now I'm defining a color palette, picking a rust-orange base with a purple-shifted default shadow, but deciding to override with explicit warmer shadow tones for key colors like RUST and RUST_DEEP to match a Genshin-style toon look.

Rounding out the palette with light/cream/belly/dark/tear/nose/stone tones, then starting the body rig by creating a builder and placing the hips joint as the root spine joint.

I'm building the spine chain with a curved path through several joints, then sweeping a body mesh along it with a radius function that varies smoothly along the length using a sine-based taper.

I'm switching to a simpler keyframe interpolation for the radii instead, with separate lerp arrays for rx and ry giving a more irregular, organic silhouette, then moving on to the fur edge paint for the body transitioning from rust to belly color.

Adjusting the boundary function so the belly patch wraps the front in a jagged, hand-painted edge, with a thin dark ink line tracing that zigzag for a stylized look. Now I'm setting up the neck joint chain, attaching it to the spine.

Still writing skeleton joints...

Still writing ear geometry...

Smoothing on convex outlines should be fine. Now I'm placing the skull as a scaled sphere positioned on the head bone, then building the muzzle as a smaller sphere offset forward, checking that its front edge sits reasonably relative to the head's front boundary.

Adding jaw and nose geometry...

Now I'm setting up eye decals by raycasting against the skull surface at symmetric azimuth angles, with a null-check fallback, plus blush decals placed lower on the cheek region using the cream paint already established for that area.

Beyond that, I'm adding cheek spike details, eyebrow dots, an ahoge tuft at the crown, and three whisker dots per side on the muzzle using small dark embedded spheres. For the mouth, I'm raycasting downward against the muzzle/jaw surfaces to find the correct placement point.

Let me simplify: center the muzzle decal at y 0.945 with height 0.05, spanning roughly 0.92-0.97, so the philtrum and smile curves land naturally against the jaw line. For the mouth texture itself I'm sketching a simple path—a short vertical philtrum line plus two curved smile strokes with small flicks at the ends—within an 80x50 viewbox, making sure the muzzle decal has enough segments (default 10) to render smoothly. With the face details settled, I'm moving on to the arms next.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry: defining hip and foot target positions, picking bone lengths that sum to more than the reach distance so the limb isn't overstretched, and setting a forward bend direction so the knee hinges correctly.

I'm setting up the leg chain with named joints parented to the hips, giving it a contact point at the foot, then starting to sweep the limb's cross-sectional radii from thigh down to ankle.

Adjusting the taper so the toe cap sinks slightly into the stone, keeping the foot section flat-bottomed with an 8-sided profile for a believable contact silhouette.

For the foot joint I'll grab the last entry in the joints array rather than risk a null tip reference, then attach three cream-colored claw spikes per foot anchored to that bone, angled forward and down from each toe position.

Now I'm laying out the arm chain with a four-point path from shoulder to hand, parenting it to the spine's third joint and tapering the radius from shoulder to wrist, with a rounded hand cap. For fingers I'm positioning three digits off the hand using local left/right offsets depending on which side the arm is on.

I'm verifying the arm roots sit inside the body's cross-section at the shoulder height, confirming the geometry checks out before moving on to building the tail chain with a catmull-rom path.

Now I'm sweeping the tail with a radius function that tapers from thick at the root to a rounded 0.028 cap at the tip, and checking the tail root position sits inside the hips' back radius correctly.

For coloring, I'm defining a banded tail tone function that alternates between rust shades with occasional dark ink accents per segment, wrapped as a paint function, and checking whether the Paint type needs an explicit import.

Then I'm scattering tail cards along the tail surface, filtering out points too close to the underside, and tinting each card using the tail tone evaluated at the nearest point on the tail path, creating a gradient tuft effect from light grey toward darker tones.

For the flow direction, I'm worried about type mismatches in the frame callback since closestT needs a point input, so I'm using the frame directly rather than accessing a nonexistent `.at` property to avoid TypeScript errors. I'm setting card sizes and lean/bend parameters appropriate for the chibi proportions before thinking about whether to add more fur cards along the cheek area.

I can index flow callbacks by position in the hits array instead, so each card or tail segment gets a precomputed direction or tangent. For cheek cards I'll tint with a cream color string, skip ear and collar fur tufts, and move on to adding moss cards with lean, bend, and spin variation parameters.

Now I'm thinking about how a stone prop should be rigged — since lathe parts need a bone reference, and only one root joint is allowed, attaching the stone directly to hips would make it move with the panda, which is wrong. A cleaner fix is to create a separate root-level joint, like "base," with hips as its child, so static props can ride the true root instead of the character's hip bone.

I need the outline point arrays typed correctly, so I'll cast them `as [number, number][]` to satisfy the tuple type rather than letting them infer as plain `number[][]`, using the same approach for the ear outlines. I'm setting the lathe segments to 9 and spin to 10, and thinking through the point ordering by distance from the axis.

For the outline profile itself, I'm keeping it low-poly with zero smoothing so corners beyond 35 degrees stay flat-shaded, which gives a nice faceted stone look at only 9 segments. I'm also planning a second smaller stone, moss clumps, and a couple tiny pebble lathes to round out the scene.

Now I'm placing small icosahedron pebbles near the base of the stone, painting them with stone material and sinking them slightly so three sit naturally outside the tail area. I'm checking that the panda's feet don't poke through the stone's top radius, and considering whether the whole build needs rescaling since a stylized chibi pose makes the proportions larger than a real red panda.

Then I'm adding glowing flower cards scattered across the hit points with a slight lean and cross pattern, applying a glow effect to them, and deciding to keep the glow subtle—skipping it on the coin emblem but maybe adding it to the bell. I'm also setting up a small gold coin cylinder for the collar, positioning it along the spine with a slight directional tilt.

Now I'm working out the coin's front emblem plane geometry—using a circle instead of a flat plane for a tighter fit, offsetting it slightly in front of the coin cylinder's face, and aligning both along the same z-axis direction so they sit flush. I'm figuring out the exact coin position by projecting from the collar ring onto the front of the body mesh.

Writing head paint shader logic...

I'm checking that paint functions return proper color types, then cleaning up unused imports like cells and smoothstep. Now I'm defining the stone palette with crack colors for the textured paint variant.

For the stone paint, I'm blending moss coverage based on surface normal and noise, with brighter moss highlights where a second noise layer crosses certain thresholds.

I'm sanity-checking that flat top surfaces always get moss coverage since the normal-based calculation pushes them well above threshold, then verifying the paint sheet's texel density is fine-grained enough (around 1.6mm per texel) given the total painted surface area across stone, body, and tail regions. I'm also noting remaining details to handle, like the mouth decal and paw toe beans.

Now I'm sketching out the SVG construction: defining a helper for placing elements on the skin using spherical coordinates, handling cheek spikes and the ahoge tuft, and checking type compatibility for the cards options (lean, bend, cross, vary, spin, color, size, etc.) and frame inputs.

I'm also working through the foot and hand joint placement, catching potential unused-variable issues before fleshing out the full build function with the atlas size and group names. Writing the main builder code...

Now I'm working through cheek spikes using the spike helper with base, direction, length and radius, then designing the ahoge tuft by building a bezier sweep curving forward from the head point outward and upward.

I'm tweaking two tufts with slightly different x-offsets for lean, applying tapered sweep radii with a flat-to-point cap transition, then moving to grouping the stone surfaces into a single rock geometry.

Scatter naturally rejects buried points inside overlapping stone meshes, which handles embedded card placement cleanly. I'm writing the collar loop and sweep setup, using the body surface's framed-up direction for the loop and a fixed-radius sweep for the neckwear group, then moving on to the tail tip and mouth decal using a hit surface combining muzzle and jaw.

Blush decals target the skull's skin surface, which accepts Surface targets fine. I'm checking chain naming conventions (left/right, ankle regex, tail parented to hips) and triangle count before finalizing the leg paint logic, which uses a zigzag pattern along the y-coordinate to color regions of the leg.

For the leg thigh boundary, I'm using rust and dark colors split by a zigzag function based on x and z coordinates to create a fur-like boundary. For the arms, I'm applying a similar zigzag split based on the cross-sectional z-coordinate to alternate between dark and rust along the tube.

Now I'm adding pebbles using flat-shaded icosahedron geometry, and moss lumps stuck onto the model with randomized embed depth, scale, and rotation, colored using a noise-based paint function that blends between moss variants. I'm finishing up by setting the eye texture size and writing the final file.
